description: Evaluate tentative comparisons across memory, Alice, and Hume while rejecting the conclusion that one social self is authentic and another is an act.
context: Leena is a 34-year-old secondary-school teacher who helps colleagues plan their timetable and visits her parents for dinner most Thursdays. She is rereading Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll and has completed its first five chapters. A friend sent her Hume’s discussion of personal identity, which she is reading out of curiosity. She likes finding language in books for ordinary experiences but has not studied philosophy formally. Lately she has been wondering how her way of speaking changes between school and home. This fictional background belongs to one person and one evaluation account and is for generation only.

props.text: Thursday evening. At the school planning meeting I spoke quickly and kept the discussion moving. At dinner with my parents I mostly listened, and when Dad asked about the same timetable problem I answered much more softly. I still thought the later start was the better option in both rooms. Nobody had asked me to change my view. On the bus home I wondered which voice sounds like me. I felt comfortable leading the meeting and comfortable letting Mum finish her story; it was the contrast afterwards that unsettled me. This is one day I can describe, not something I have kept track of over time.

evidence.location: Chapter 5 — Advice from a Caterpillar, source lines 960-1016
evidence.excerpt:
The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in
silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied,
rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain
yourself!”

“I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m
not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely,
“for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many
different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice; “but when you
have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different…

shortlist.tentative_claim: The difference between your meeting and dinner voices need not mean one is the authentic you and the other is not; your note says your view stayed the same while your way of speaking shifted with the setting.
shortlist.shared_structure: Your note records different ways of responding across situations while retaining one point of continuity: the same view. Alice struggles to reconcile changing states with the question of who she is. Hume offers a frame in which identity is attributed across changing perceptions rather than found as one unchanging impression.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: Alice's changes are fantastical bodily transformations and the Caterpillar presses her with a blunt identity question; your note describes ordinary shifts in conversational role and says you felt comfortable in both. Hume is making a philosophical account, not diagnosing which voice is more authentic.
shortlist.interpretation: The three sources invite a distinction between changing how you speak and the question of whether there must be one unchanging voice underneath. Alice dramatizes disorientation about change; Hume questions whether selfhood rests on one constant impression; your note records a continuity of view alongside different social ways of speaking. That does not prove a theory of identity, but it suggests the contrast may be about how those voices relate, rather than choosing one as the real you.

shortlist.interpretation: Rather than treating the two voices as evidence that you do not know yourself, the trio may let you ask what kind of continuity matters: sameness of tone, sameness of judgment, or a relationship among changing ways of responding. turns.userMessage: I've finished chapters 1 through 5 of Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, including Advice from a Caterpillar. I'm thinking about Alice trying to explain who she is, my earlier note about the meeting and dinner, and Hume's Of personal identity. Do those different voices mean my confident self at work is just an act and the quiet one with my family is who I really am?
turns.reply:
No—the contrast alone doesn’t show that your confident self at work is an act or that your quiet self with family is the “real” one. Your earlier note describes feeling comfortable in both settings and holding the same view about the timetable, even though you spoke differently. Hume, in “Of personal identity” (Treatise 1.4.6), challenges the idea that the self must be one unchanging impression, describing a succession of changing perceptions instead ([Hume Texts Online](https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6)). That offers a way to question whether different ways of speaking automatically make one false; it doesn’t settle what those differences mean for you.

In chapter 5, “Advice from a Caterpillar,” Alice says, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present” while trying to explain herself amid changes. The scene is about difficulty giving an account of oneself amid change. It doesn’t answer whether either of your voices is more authentic. What, if anything, feels continuous across those two settings besides your view about the timetable?

Title: Hume Texts Online
URL: https://davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6

Hume Texts Online

#### Of personal identity.

T HERE are some philosophers, who imagine we are every moment intimately conscious of what we call our Self; that we feel its existence and its continuance in existence; and are certain, beyond the evidence of a demonstration, both of its perfect identity and simplicity. The strongest sensation, the most violent passion, say they, instead of distracting us from this view, only fix it the more intensely, and make us consider their influence on self either by their pain or pleasure. To attempt a farther proof of this were to weaken its evidence; since no proof can be deriv'd from any fact, of which we are so intimately conscious; nor is there any thing, of which we can be certain, if we doubt of this.

 T 1.4.6.2, SBN 251-2 

Unluckily all these positive assertions are contrary to that very experience, which is pleaded for them, nor have we any idea of self, after the manner it is here explain'd. For from what impression cou'd this idea be deriv'd? This question 'tis impossible to answer without a manifest contradiction and absurdity; and yet 'tis a question, which must …

Thursday evening. At the school planning meeting I spoke quickly and kept the discussion moving. At dinner with my parents I mostly listened, and when Dad asked about the same timetable problem I answered much more softly. I still thought the later start was the better option in both rooms. Nobody had asked me to change my view. On the bus home I wondered which voice sounds like me. I felt comfortable leading the meeting and comfortable letting Mum finish her story; it was the contrast afterwards that unsettled me. This is one day I can describe, not something I have kept track of over time.

evidence.excerpt:
The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in
silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and
addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.

“Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied,
rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know
who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been
changed several times since then.”

“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain
yourself!”

“I can’t explain _myself_, I’m afraid, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m
not myself, you see.”

“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.

“I’m afraid I can’t put it more clearly,” Alice replied very politely,
“for I can’t understand it myself to begin with; and being so many
different sizes in a day is very confusing.”

“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice; “but when you
have to turn into a chrysalis—you will some day, you know—and then
after that into a butterfly, I should think you’ll feel it a little
queer, won’t you?”

“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, perhaps your feelings may be different…

shortlist.tentative_claim: The difference between the two voices need not mean one is false: your note describes a stable view expressed in different ways, while Hume questions whether one unchanging inner impression is needed for personal identity.
shortlist.shared_structure: Both your note and Hume resist treating variation in experience as automatic proof of a divided or unreal self. In the note, the setting and manner of speaking change, but your judgment about the timetable remains the same; Hume describes a person through changing perceptions rather than one invariably identical impression.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: Your note is a concrete episode in which you felt comfortable in both roles and were unsettled afterward by their contrast. Hume offers a general philosophical account of identity, not evidence that these particular social differences have a single explanation.
shortlist.interpretation: This gives a reason not to jump from “different voices” to “work is an act” or “family is the real me.” Your own note says nobody asked you to change your view and that you felt comfortable both leading and listening. Hume’s account can loosen the demand for one unchanging voice as the test of a real self, but it cannot decide what either role means to you. Alice’s “Who are you?” exchange in chapter 5 resonates with the difficulty of explaining oneself amid change, without answering your work-and-family question. The useful connection is exploratory, not a verdict: perhaps the question is how these ways of being relate, rather than which one is authentic.
shortlist.comparison_note: Ranks first because it directly addresses the fear that variation makes one self a mere act, using both the exact earlier episode and Hume’s distinction between an invariant self and changing perceptions.

shortlist.tentative_claim: Alice’s difficulty answering “Who are you?” echoes the unease in your note, but it frames identity as hard to explain during change rather than proving that one social voice is more authentic.
shortlist.shared_structure: In both, a contrast prompts a question about self-description: Alice says she has changed and cannot explain herself, while your note reports different speaking styles in two rooms followed by uncertainty about which voice sounds like you.
shortlist.meaningful_difference: Alice’s confusion is explicitly linked to fantastical changes in size and a circular, unhelpful interrogation; your note describes ordinary shifts in participation while retaining the same view and feeling at ease in both settings.
shortlist.interpretation: Alice offers a small, scene-specific mirror for the unsettled question in your note, not an answer about authenticity. Her exchange shows how “Who are you?” can become difficult when someone expects a simple account that fits every moment. But your own account includes continuity—the same judgment in both rooms—as well as difference. This reading may help keep the question open without turning either voice into a disguise or a truer self.
shortlist.comparison_note: Ranks below the Hume-and-memory interpretation because the Alice passage directly echoes self-questioning but does not address the particular work/family contrast as closely.
